Mamadou Konaté est un «ange gardien». Il: Mamadou Konaté is a “guardian angel.” He worked as a cleaner in a long-term care home (CHSLD). He was on the front lines from the start of the health crisis. Because he has no status in Canada, he is now threatened with deportation.
Mamadou est malheureusement un exemple p: Mamadou is unfortunately one of many front-line workers living in insecurity because they lack status. His application for permanent residence on humanitarian grounds was refused, so all he can do now is wait for a review or hope for regularization.
Cette situation a été dénoncée par les o: This situation was denounced by the organizers of an emergency vigil held on Wednesday, September 23, outside the Passport Canada offices on René-Lévesque Boulevard. Mamadou Konaté had been placed in the Immigration Prevention Centre (CPI) in Laval, and a hearing was being held that same day to decide on his release.
Des proches et des citoyens que l’histoi: Loved ones and citizens moved by Mamadou’s story organized the vigil to demand his release from the centre. But he was not released. “He failed to show up once in February 2019, so they judged that he was not reliable,” says his lawyer, Stewart Istvanffy. “One of the people [at the hearing] claimed that she didn’t know him well enough.”
« Statut pour tous et toutes. Personne n: “Status for all! No one is illegal!” and “Solidarity with the undocumented” were the chants of activists and supporters at the vigil. Participants not only defended Mamadou but also denounced the situation of foreign workers who worked in essential sectors during the health crisis. So far, these guardian angels have received nothing but thanks. And many of them have no legal status in the country, like Mamadou, who is a refugee.
Il avait un visa de travail fermé lié au: He had a closed work permit tied to the CHSLD that employed him, which made him a temporary worker. “He worked right up until he was detained. He told me he wanted to go back to work tomorrow, if he could,” Istvanffy said at a press conference on September 25.
Pour répondre à cet enjeu et aux revendi: To address this issue and the demands of civil society, the Quebec and Canadian governments reached an agreement on August 13 providing for the creation of a program to regularize people without status who worked in the health care sector. But this open door to permanent residence will not be accessible to all the foreign workers considered essential during COVID-19.
Les critères énoncés ne permettront qu’à: The stated criteria will allow fewer than a thousand people to obtain their papers. To be eligible, a person must be an asylum seeker and have worked a certain number of hours directly with patients. Maintenance workers like Mamadou, and security guards, are therefore not entitled to benefit from the regularization program for health care guardian angels, which, let’s repeat, is for now intended solely for care staff.
Nous avons écrit à Immigration, Réfugiés: We wrote to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to learn more about the possibility of broadening the criteria. Béatrice Fénelon, the department’s spokesperson, reminded us of the terms of the measure, which is a “one-time initiative [that] comes with very specific criteria recognizing the service of workers in the health care sector, where there is an urgent need for help and where they are putting their own lives at risk to care for others.”
Mamadou Konaté est arrivé au Québec en: Mamadou Konaté arrived in Quebec in 2016. He wanted to live, study and work far from war, having been taken prisoner during one of the armed conflicts that have torn apart his country, Côte d’Ivoire, since 2002. Here, he learned French and got involved with community organizations. He worked at a recycling centre, in the forests of Northern Quebec and, most recently, in a CHSLD. It was there that he worked as a cleaner in contaminated areas, on the front lines alongside the sick. He caught COVID-19 in April and had to fend for himself, with no support from the government. Once he recovered, he went back to work.
« Des amis m’ont dit que Mamadou avait d: “Friends told me Mamadou was having a hard time, so I helped him during his quarantine. That’s how I met him. He put his life at risk for people like me, and now the government wants to deport him,” Mathieu said indignantly at the emergency vigil. His loved ones have rallied to support him through his ordeal, including this Wednesday, September 23, the day of the review hearing at which a decision on his release from the CPI was to be made. They are demanding Mamadou’s release, the cancellation of the deportation notice and a review of the decision on his permanent residence.
Reconnu comme réfugié par les Nations un: Recognized as a refugee by the United Nations and the Red Cross, Mamadou had applied for permanent residence on humanitarian grounds, submitting a complete file that included letters of support and evidence confirming his difficult past. But his application was rejected. “We’re still waiting for the reasons, but we suspect he was found inadmissible because he was a member of a group that tried to overthrow a government by force [that of Côte d’Ivoire, Ed.].
Je ne suis pas d’accord avec ce genre d’: I don’t agree with that kind of accusation. If we refuse residence to someone who tried to overthrow a repressive government, it means we’re backing the worst governments in the world. Our law is badly made,” says Stewart Istvanffy.
Le 19 septembre, après avoir reçu son av: On September 19, after receiving his deportation notice, he went voluntarily with his lawyer to the CPI to have his deportation suspended and to request a review of his residence application. That is how he ended up in the centre.

Parmi les travailleurs étrangers qui se: Among the foreign workers who proved essential during the health crisis, we must mention temporary workers. “They do jobs we wouldn’t do, like in agriculture. If they weren’t here, we wouldn’t eat. I’ve worked in the agricultural sector with temporary foreign workers, and I was really in the minority. Nine-tenths of the employees there are foreign, Latin American. Honestly, I had a hard time keeping up with them. They’re used to working 16 hours a day, and I could barely do my 8 hours,” Mathieu said.
« Mamadou est un bon ami à moi. On s’es: “Mamadou is a good friend of mine. We met through friends, and we had business projects together. More broadly, I don’t agree with what the government is doing. False promises were made to workers like Mamadou. He has been waiting for status for four years. I’m extremely disappointed, because we also know that his work is essential.
Comme lui, beaucoup de travailleurs ont: Like him, many workers had high hopes after those promises of regularization,” Arielle said indignantly at the vigil for Mamadou Konaté. To her, his detention is absurd when you consider his work history or his residence file. She would like him to be released from the Laval centre, at the very least, so he can protect himself from the second wave of COVID-19 arriving in Quebec.
Les conditions sanitaires au CPI font en: Sanitary conditions at the CPI do raise fears for his safety. Abdul, who is also undocumented, was placed in the Laval centre earlier during the health crisis. “The government was talking about physical distancing measures, but we didn’t see them applied at the centre. With other detainees, we started a hunger strike to demand respectful detention conditions. We suffered a lot. But after 10 days, they released us, me and almost everyone else, on conditions. Today, I’m still out on conditional release,” he said during the vigil.
Abdul est originaire du Sénégal, et sa d: Abdul is originally from Senegal, and his asylum claim was refused earlier this year. He was summoned to receive a removal notice. Lost and without a lawyer, he decided not to go and ended up being arrested and placed in the CPI. “I’m here for Mamadou, but also because it could be me in a little while. I’m waiting for my application to be reviewed,” he continued. Abdul, who is also undocumented, was placed in the Laval centre earlier during the health crisis.
Lors de l’audience où l’on devait statue: At the hearing where a decision on Mamadou Konaté’s release was to be made, no mention of COVID-19 was allowed. “It was a crazy hearing, we couldn’t say anything about the pandemic,” his lawyer, Stewart Istvanffy, recalled. He says, however, that Mamadou has been in quarantine since arriving at the centre and that his detention conditions are acceptable for now. On the recommendation of Béatrice Fénelon of IRCC, we wrote to the Canada Border Services Agency, which is responsible for the Laval centre, to find out what health measures are applied there, but we received no response.
« La suite des choses dépend en grande p: “What happens next depends largely on politics,” Istvanffy said on September 24, as Québec solidaire took up the case to bring it to Quebec’s Minister of Immigration, Nadine Girault. The next day, MNAs Andrés Fontecilla and Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois held a press conference in front of the Complexe Guy-Favreau and the Passport Canada offices, together with Istvanffy. They appealed to the government’s sense of responsibility and humanity. “Quebec needs him. A guardian angel is being treated like a criminal, and that is unacceptable.
Au lieu de le déporter, on devrait le re: Instead of deporting him, we should thank him by granting him permanent status. The Quebec government needs to get involved to fix this serious injustice,” said Andrés Fontecilla, MNA for Laurier-Dorion. Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois, MNA for Gouin, called for the Minister of Immigration to intervene “within the next few hours to stop this senseless deportation.” “Quebec must give Mr. Konaté a CSQ [Quebec Selection Certificate],” he then hammered home.
